utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would remind you the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Now Mr. Djordjevic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Peraj, good morning. I'm Dragoljub Djordjevic, attorney at law, Defence counsel for the accused Vlastimir Djordjevic, and I would like to put some questions to you. I hope that through them we will be able to better explain the situation in terms of the facts concerning everything that you have stated so far in all ways, written statements, oral statements, testimony and so on and so forth. Mr. Peraj, first of all, I would be interested in your personal details. First of all, I would like to hear what your wife's name is, where she is from, from what town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think -- although I rise with regret, but I think if we're going to proceed in that direction, counsel first needs to indicate to the Court what possible relevance the domestic affairs of the witness could be to the issues in this case. Secondly, counsel needs to consider whether or not wherever he's going, if it is at all appropriate, should be done in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I appreciate what Mr. Stamp said, Your Honour. However, the questions that I'm going to put are not of a nature that would require closed session. The questions are such so that we would get a general impression as to where he lived, how he lived, what he did, and under what conditions he later left the Army of Yugoslavia, I mean Mr. Peraj. Those are the reasons why my questions are moving in that direction. As for the broader context, I assume that my colleague Mr. Stamp is going to interrupt me several times. That is what I wish to say at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, the Chamber is not persuaded that there would be in this line of questioning anything of sufficient relevance to justify the time it would take. We are interested in learning about the facts of -- that are relevant to this case. If there was some very particular issue about the personal life of the witness in general terms, that might be different, but a general examination is something which seems to the Chamber to be quite beyond what we would value hearing. So if you could move on to some other area of questioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Trial Chamber has ruled, so I'm not going to go into the reasons that led me to adopt this line of questioning. However, I'm going to move on in a far more direct manner than until now, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness tell us how many brothers and sisters he has and where they were in 1999, whether they were in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order for you to understand my line of questioning, my question is whether any of the witness's close relatives or distant relatives were members of the KLA. When I ask this, my question is actually put in relation to his more distant relatives, his brothers-in-law and so on. We hear that the witness is from Ramoc, and my question is in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I expect to hear your answer. I don't know if you've heard the question.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear the question. I have four brothers, four sisters. My father died in the year 2000. My mother is still alive. One brother and his sons lived in Dallashaj during the war, and he still lives there now, while the three other brothers were not in Kosovo at all during the war because they live and work in Switzerland. This is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The second part of my question was whether any of your distant relatives or close relatives were members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one from my family was ever a member of the KLA. As regards distant relatives, I don't know. If you mean distant relatives, the extended family, well, it would be a long story.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, sir, Mr. Peraj. Let us clarify something. There seem to have been several problems in relation to your question that Mr. Pal Gjokaj or Paul Gjokaj. I'm not sure because in the transcripts we have different names that appear, and in your statements too. Let me remind you, this is a person who said you conveyed your information that the terrorists of the KLA would be attacked in the village of Ramoc. Later on, you said that that was the reason why they did not liquidate you, I mean the members of the KLA. "Most probably," those were your words. But who is Mr. Gjoklaj? Is he related to you at all? You did say something, and you kept saying that he was a brother-in-law or something to that effect. Let us try to clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Pal Gjoklaj never informed me personally where the KLA units were. Secondly, Pal Gjoklaj is [Realtime transcript read in error, "not"] my wife's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's not my question. That was not my question. I'm asking you about the part of the statement that you gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm just wondering as a matter of the record. I see here at line 17, "Pal Gjoklaj is not my wife's brother." When I think I heard a translation in the positive. I think. I might have been wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We didn't heard translation in B/C/S. I'm talking because of my client, what Mr. Stamp said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just carry on, please, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So please, Mr. Peraj, could you enunciate his name very specifically now because we really want to have his right name in the transcript. It's Gjoklaj, it's Gjokaj, it's Pal, it's other things, so could you please slowly enunciate his name so we that have it for the record?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see here on the transcript, although I don't read English, but it's correct in the transcript: Pal Gjoklaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Excellent. My next question: You stated in your statement that he is your wife's brother; is that correct, your wife's brother?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In our language there's an expression for that, I mean in B/C/S. The word is "surak" in B/C/S. That is brother-in-law, wife's brother. So you will agree that "surak" would be the right word for that particular relationship; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, yes. "Surak" means the wife's brother. So my wife's brother in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: To go back what I had said, you mentioned to this person, your brother-in-law, your surak, that there would be an action against the KLA and that this had to do with the village of Ramoc. Yesterday, you explained that there's a village called Madanaj right next to Ramoc and that's where the forces were. You did not have full knowledge about this. You said that there was no KLA in Ramoc. So could you tell me, why did you say to your wife's brother that on the following day or whenever, an action was being prepared against the KLA? What was the point of that message?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the villages Madanaj and Ramoc are next to each other. The place where the KLA soldiers were is very close to the house of Pal Gjoklaj. Previously, the KLA soldiers were not there at all, not even close to that area. I received information from several people that they were there. This was at the beginning of June 1999. After the massacres in Meje and Korenice, a lot of blood had been shed. Many people had been killed, and these people had gone there to be closer to Gjakove, in order to enter Gjakove, because the Kumanovo agreement had been signed for the withdrawal of the forces from Kosova. For this reason, it had been planned for all of them to be liquidated together with 40 civilians that had been together with them, people who had been in the mountains and had survived the Meje massacre; and for that reason, knowing what kind of massacre had happened there, I thought that these people should not die in vain. And if this action would take place, some families that were in the Ramoc village, ten families altogether, would suffer. At that time, almost everything was over, the war was over, and that is the reason why I informed Pal Gjoklaj to tell them to leave the place they were in at the time. This is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, you said that at that time the Kumanovo agreements had already been signed. It is a generally known fact, and therefore, I'm not going to show you any documents in relation to this particular matter, but we all know that immediately after the Kumanovo agreement was signed, the army and the police of Serbia withdraw from -- withdrew from the area, especially from the area of Djakovica. So logistically, they started preparing for withdrawal straight away. They started withdrawing their materiel and technical resources. That is the right expression for all the resources of this kind that an army has. You were a member of the army, so I'm sure that you're familiar with it. So I would like to know about these activities in June. It was clear to everyone that the army and the police and the paramilitaries were withdrawing at the time since NATO forces were entering. So that's my first question. Why was this done, and where did you get information about the presence of the KLA in that area? How did you come about such information?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day when the people who were there would be attacked in the evening, I met Dragan Pekovic, who was a postman. He was, in fact, a guardsman at the post office. His son, Aleksandar Pekovic, was a policeman, and Dragan asked me whether I would take part in the action in the evening. I said to him that I didn't know anything about any action. What kind of action are you talking about, I asked him. He told me that, This is the last time that my son will take part in such an action, and that if his son would survive this action, nothing would happen to him anymore, so in the meaning that his son would not die in action. This is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did the postman know you personally?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's my neighbour in Dallashaj. He lived there since he was a child. We've been neighbours, and we've been very close. Then he went to live in Piskote. He worked as a postman in the village of Skivjan. Our children know each other as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: He asked you whether you were prepared to go into action in the village of Ramoc where your closest relatives live, where your closest family members live; right? That's what he asked you?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan asked me, Are you going to take part in the action tonight in the evening? And I asked him, What are you talking about; I never took part in any action. And he told me all the details that I explained to you. He told me about the members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It would be clearer to me if he had said to you, There's going to be an action; try to get your own people out, your own family members. But I don't really understand this. But never mind, that's your answer. Now you're referring to a part of your statement that is in paragraph 105 where you describe this particular event. The second part of my question was: How was it you knew, first of all, that there was some KLA Brigade out there? How did you know that personally? And how did you have very specific information about this brigade, namely that there were 126 members in uniform and 40 volunteers? This is the very beginning of paragraph 105. You say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. We cannot follow him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not interpret what was read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're going too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could put a short question, and the interpreters can take it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I'm looking at the transcript now to see what was in the transcript at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The reference to paragraph 105, that was read out very fast. That's what we didn't interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said in paragraph 105 in the beginning of June 1999, the Army of Yugoslavia and the MUP surrounded in Ramoc the 137th Brigade of the KLA, about 126 uniformed members and 40 volunteers. That is the very beginning of paragraph 105 of your statement. I'm asking you the following: How do you know at that moment that the KLA was in Ramoc, in that village; and secondly, how is it that you have this very specific information like 126 uniformed members and 40 volunteers? That is the first part of my question.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned this later from Pal Gjoklaj and some other people who were there in the 137th Brigade. I mean, they told me about the numbers, the 126 and the 40 people. When I went to Pal Gjoklaj to tell him and warn him, I didn't know the numbers, but a couple of days later I learnt the number of people that were there. After the war, I heard the same thing about the number of people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of what kind of a military formation it was, the figures, especially during the war, are strictly confidential. Could you please tell me whether Pal Gjoklaj gave you -- gave you this information because you worked as some kind of an intelligence officer for the Army of Yugoslavia, or was it in some other context? Could you please explain that. What other context could it be for these exact figures to be given to you, and why is it important at all after everything is said and done? What is the nature of your contact with Pal Gjoklaj, and what was the context in which this exact figure for volunteers and uniformed persons was -- were given to you? I think that it should be treated as top secret for such a military formation during the war. So in what context were you talking about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would kindly ask you to instruct the counsel to ask me short and clearly defined questions, not three, four, five questions at once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's a valid point, Mr. Djordjevic. If you look, you've got about, in the transcript, ten lines in which you have indicated three or four different things you want to inquire about. I think it would help everybody if you could just deal with them one at a time and just go through it that way rather than put the whole picture with a number of questions all at once. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will comply to the extent in which it is possible, but in this situation where I asked this question over ten lines or a few questions, I did it in a way which I deemed to be necessary, but let me try to rephrase it to make it as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me, Mr. Gjoklaj -- or, rather, Mr. Peraj, that at that time the information about the strength of the 137th Brigade of the Kosovo Liberation Army should have been treated as a military secret given that there was a state of war? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the Yugoslav Army, for the MUP, yes, it would be a military secret, but not for this. I don't see any secrecy here. They were 126 members and 40 volunteers. I don't know why it would constitute a secret for him to tell me. He told me that this was the case. Now, as to whether he gave away the secrets of the KLA or not, that is of no relevance to me. This is my answer. I will continue with another question that you asked. Pal Gjoklaj and some others told me later that what I did was in fact very good because these people survived, and they didn't [microphone not activated] at risk, and they didn't undertake any military action. You may call them terrorists. Maybe I can call them terrorists, too, but they had their own name: The Kosovo Liberation Army. We can call them as we wish, but this is what they were called.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, you were an officer of the Yugoslav Army. Did you take an oath of loyalty to that organisation that you belonged to? Did you take an oath?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did take an oath, but this was not an oath for me to work against the constitution of former Yugoslavia or against the international convention, because Yugoslavia was a signatory of these international conventions, and if you abide by them you should not kill people on the streets. They did not undertake any actions. They had free hands to imprison them all and treat them as POWs but not execute them. Excuse me, but I have the right to refuse to carry out such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that later. You're now wasting our precious time. This is not about refusing to obey orders. Please don't go out of the context of my questions. I asked you whether you took an oath and you said yes. So my next question -- please, please. So we are agreed. I promised that I would be concise and brief. So could you please give me brief answers and have some respect for the time that we all here in the courtroom have because if you answer outside of what I asked you, then it just makes no sense. Nobody said that civilians should get killed. We are now talking about the KLA, and that's why I'm asking you this. You took an oath. At that time, you were a member of the Army of Yugoslavia. You tell Pal Gjoklaj that the KLA should get out of there because an action was underway. I want to ask you this: Who did you work for at the time? So we have one military force, the Kosovo Liberation Army, the KLA, whatever it's called, and we have another force, the Yugoslav Army. At that time, the Yugoslav Army is directly confronted -- it confronts the KLA in a war. So now I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you're now getting into another extremely long speech. You asked a question, whether the witness whether he had taken an oath. He has said yes. I think your next question is: "Were you at that time a member of the Yugoslav Army," and the witness has yet had an opportunity -- not yet had an opportunity to answer that. If you can see what I mean? Just get to the point to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, please, please. Before I go on, I will, of course, comply with everything that you've just told me, but I would like to ask the witness to answer my questions the way I ask them because the witness is moving away from the context, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's why I've intervened. You're not just asking a question; you're making a speech, putting in lots of facts that you want to be understood. You need to put a short question to the witness and get from the witness an answer, yes or no. If you agree with the answer, you move on to your next question. If you don't agree with the answer, you can ask something else about that. Okay? We really must move on dealing specifically with short questions if we're to get anywhere. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is crystal clear to me, but I don't get specific answers, so I have to apologise for being long-winded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Yugoslav Army at that time? Did you at that time collaborate with the Kosovo Liberation Army - that's in early June - or no?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the former Yugoslav Army. I did not collaborate with the UCK or KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell Pal Gjoklaj that an action was in the offing and that the KLA should pull out from that area?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't consider that to be tantamount to collaboration with the KLA and giving away military secrets of the Army of Yugoslavia? I'm talking about only the KLA here.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of what I had seen in Meje, in Korenice, and other places, at that moment I was not at all interested in the fact of whether they were KLA or terrorists or whatever. They were human beings to me. I didn't want anyone to die in vain. I helped people who were of Serb and Montenegrin ethnicity too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is this: Were you able to inform only the civilians that they should take shelter because there was an action about to be launched by the Yugoslav Army? Could you have done that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed him for the whole group, the civilians that were together with the Brigade that met the Brigade in the mountains. These 40 persons were persons who escaped from the convoy on the 27th of April. Therefore, I told Pal to inform them, the group, so that they could leave and not remain there. Otherwise, they will be liquidated. I even told him where they can take shelter and survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Those were your neighbours, villagers from the village where you yourself were born. You explained to the Judges that you used your authority to prevent the execution of 12 of your fellow countrymen, people of the same ethnic background, and you mentioned the Scepanovic and others. Could you have done the same thing now to protect the civilians as you had done on that occasion using your authority?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilians were together with the KLA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, you said that there were 40 volunteers in addition to 126 uniformed members. Does it mean that the 40 volunteers were not in uniforms? Am I correct if I understand it in that way?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "volunteer" is not correct in this context. They were not volunteers as such. They were volunteers to join their family to wherever they went. They met the KLA members in the mountains, and the KLA took them under their care so that they could help them with food and everything else. I wouldn't call them proper volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What would you call them?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would in fact call them lost, people without hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were they actually members of the KLA, or were they volunteers? Because I assume that elements of the KLA were organised on a voluntary basis at that time, or can we say at that time it was already a professionally organised army?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment they left their families and took to the mountains in order to avoid the check-point, these persons, in my opinion, are not persons who joined the KLA. Even if we assume they were volunteers or they were armed, that would not be a big deal in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, your opinion is quite clear to me. I will not be asking any more questions about that. Let me go back to your brother-in-law, Pal Gjoklaj, that person who attended some of your interviews when you gave statements after the Yugoslav Army pulled out of Kosovo. So Pal or Paul Gjoklaj, was he present when you were giving those statements?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pal Gjoklaj was present. I was in his house. Pal Gjoklaj is an English teacher, and to be honest, he helped the translator, the interpreter, with certain terms. He -- the interpreter, was young, not very experienced, so he helped with the terminology. Pal Gjoklaj did not have any other influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As regards the written statements that you gave to the KLA members immediately after the pull-out of the army and the police, do you remember doing that? Do you remember giving a written statement to the KLA members at any time?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true. I don't remember the details. Ten years have passed since.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And was your brother-in-law Gjoklaj also present when those statements were being given or written down?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. And was Pal Gjoklaj a member of the KLA or a volunteer or anything of the sort?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you with full responsibility that he was not a KLA member, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe a supporter, yes, but that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have this statement in front of you in hard copy, so I won't call it up on the screen. Could you please look at paragraph 5 of that statement. Could you please explain that: "When I arrived in Djakovica the situation was already degenerated." It's the very beginning of paragraph 5. "The VJ army units occupied the territory of Djakovica municipality. VJ forces --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The counsel is kindly asked to slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So I'm not going to explain all of that. So my question to you is: To "take" or "occupy" in military jargon means to wrest the territory away from the enemy, and since this is what it looks like, now I would like you to ask explain to me who was it that the VJ took the territory of the Gjakove municipality from? Of course, we're talking about your statement of the 8 and 9th of August, 2006, and that's P313.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The formulation is not correct of this one word. They took positions in the entire territory of Gjakove municipality. This is what I tried to say. They were dislocated in all the Gjakove municipality territory. The army was already there, so there's no logic to occupy something that they already possess.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And what does it mean the situation had already deteriorated?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, the situation deteriorated. Sporadic actions were ongoing on the part of the KLA against the army and police members. Moreover, the deployment of police and paramilitary forces there and reservist forces who committed wrong-doings - I'm now speaking about the time-period of December 1998 - this is what I meant by the situation deteriorated. It didn't look that it was going to get any better but worse, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, it's much clearer now. Paragraph 6, Colonel Milos Djosan. Who is that? What's your relationship with him? What was he doing at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos Djosan was the commander of the brigade where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was your answer, but my question has, first of all, to do with the relationship that you had as a captain first class. That was your rank; right? And in light of that rank that you held, how much contact did you have with Colonel Djosan at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say everyday contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Direct contact or through his subordinates such as, for instance, Mr. Stankovic, his deputy?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both direct and through his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who were you in contact with in that period? Who was your immediate superior? That's what I'm talking about. Djosan, Stankovic, who else?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Novica Stankovic, too, who was the chief of the brigade staff. There was another first class captain from Leskovac. I don't remember his name. He also worked in the same brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, according to your statement, you transported the bodies of the soldiers to Pristina, Nis, and wherever it was that you were taking them. How had those guys got killed? You said over 40, that you yourself transported over 40 of them. Soldiers, I'm talking about soldiers.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These soldiers were killed mainly in the border area, and on two or three occasions - I'm not quite sure how many - during NATO bombing when they targeted the radars -- correction, radar, I know of a case when eight soldiers and a non-commissioned officer were killed as they entered a minefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me, Mr. Milos Djosan, during the action that you're talking about, the action that you label a massacre, was Djosan your immediate superior at that time too?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned it earlier that at that time he was commander of the Brigade I was a part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Talking about international conventions, and I can see that you're quite familiar with them. In light of the circumstances, as a member of the Army of Yugoslavia and as a human being, did you ever report terrible crimes, atrocities against civilians in Meje, Meje-Orize, Korenica, and other locations where you claim they happened? Did you report that to Milos Djosan so that he could take appropriate measures against the perpetrators and attempt to identify them?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not report to him because together with me was the person whose task it was to report to him, and I think that he must have reported what happened to Djosan. Other people, too, must have told him what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, you're an officer of the Army of Yugoslavia, an Albanian. Didn't you feel it was necessary for you to do this personally in respect of your commander?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not inform him directly. Whether you believe me or not, what can I do? I had friendly contacts with Milos Djosan. I met him. I had met him before, and Milos Djosan is a good person. He was a good person. He had a good heart, and he told me -- please, I would apologise here, but I will say this in Serbo-Croatian: Peraj, what is happening is so sad, it cannot be sadder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what more can I report to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, precisely because of what you said, that you're in daily contact with him. You see him every day. That's what you stated a few moments ago in relation to my question, and that's why I'm asking you, was it not possible that you didn't indicate this to him? And then my next question: Do you know if this man initiated many proceedings against persons who committed crimes in that territory for rape, theft, arson? Do you know that? Were you aware of that since you say that you were in daily contact with him, you were well informed? That's why I'm asking you this.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of several things, and that's why I mentioned here that he was not a bad person. He was a good man generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you did not take part in any fighting. Is that correct? You said that you didn't take part in a single action.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the day of my birth until this day -- I'm sorry. From the day I was born to this day, today, here, I never participated in any military action or police action.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain to me part of your statement, or perhaps I should say the last one. You said several times that in accordance with the law, all participants in any operations during the war are resubordinated to the army. You said that that is what the law says. What law did you mean, if you can tell me. If not, could you at least try to give all of us a description as to what you meant?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I think I corrected something here, but in the beginning I based myself on the principle that used to be in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let's me just remind you. Later on, you spoke about this in detail, that some people were not interested in anything any longer and that they moved away from the military. We'll get to that. But I just wanted to know what you meant by this resubordination to the Army of Yugoslavia in a war situation. Could you just deal with that briefly? Then we are going to move on to this other matter.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this term you're using, "resubordination," because in Albanian it doesn't make any sense as a term. If you could use the Serbo-Croatian term.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The gist of this question is as follows: During the war, during the days of the war, the police is resubordinated to the army of Yugoslavia, the Territorial Defence, the civilian protection. That's the system of defence that you described, as well, that existed in the former Yugoslavia. I am just asking you to explain that. What did that mean, namely that everyone has to be subordinated or resubordinated to the army when there is a war situation, and, indeed, there was a law to that effect.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My line of thinking was that if the operational staff, the commander of which, "verhovni" in Serbo-Croatian, the Supreme Commander, he's the head of the state, and if the staff reaches the conclusion that it is necessary for some units to join other forces in operations that would take place, they decided sometimes that certain police units would be subordinated to army units. This is what I was thinking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, did you have a particular reference in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely what I wish to point out. [In English] Right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 10 of your statement, P313, paragraph 11, it says in paragraph 11 there was a war that -- there was a law that said that during the war other structures should be resubordinated to the Army of Yugoslavia. It says here that you are thinking along your own train of thought, but you know this. And then 11, paragraph 11: "The MUP was subordinated to the main commanders of the Army of Yugoslavia. This was strictly on the basis of an agreement."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these are the references in relation to the question I've been putting. I've asked the witness what he thinks, what he knows. If that's it, then that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is where I made the correction because MUP is a separate organisation. There could be coordination of actions and operations between the two organisations, but never said that MUP was commanded by the Yugoslav Army, and I think I made that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you do that only now? Why is this the first time, in fact, that you're doing it?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that it was a mistake because it's just one word and it changes the whole meaning. It's not even a sentence, just one word that changes it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you, Mr. Peraj, because this is the first trial of a police general. But, all right, I accept the amendment that you made only now. It is 11 years later that your memory has been refreshed. Further on, you speak of paramilitary units. It is all within the main topic that is called "Armed Groups Overview I." And then you say in paragraph 12 -- now I shall be moving on from one paragraph to another because obviously you don't remember what it was that you had stated. You talk about the Territorial Defence that operates together with the MUP, and then you talk about Arkan's Tigers, Seselj's White Eagles, then Franko Simatovic, the Frenki's. You believe that all of them are paramilitary units; right? I didn't hear your answer. Frenki's men, the Tigers, the White Eagles, are they all paramilitary units? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: You say that these units were subordinated to the MUP, right, these paramilitaries units? Am I right when I say that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: MUP supported and coordinated their actions with them. I saw that with my own eyes, both in Meje, but especially in Meje, and in town. One other explanation: Had MUP and the army not accepted them, these forces would have fought against them because they were criminals, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you agree with me, then, that these units in fact evaded both military and police control and that they acted on their own, these criminals. Can you just answer?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with what you said, that they also carried out independent operations, but nobody hindered them. Nobody stopped them, and that is the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At any rate, in your view they are what is meant when one says "paramilitary," but then you're talking about the police and the military who did not stop them. When you say "paramilitary," if we look at the etymology of the word, there is the military, and we're talking about the police. So they can be paramilitary. You believe that it can mean para-police as well. When somebody says paramilitary to me, I think that they're referring to something that may be the military but not necessarily. I would like to hear your comments, if any, in respect of this.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you to some extent because in the army, especially in the brigade where I was working, some -- such forces came under the pretext that they had been sent by the defence ministry of Yugoslavia to help us, and in fact they were members of Seselj's party, Arkan's party, and Vuk Draskovic's party. So there was this suspicion that they had been in agreement to send paramilitary forces to help the army and the police. They did not stay long in the army, though, not even a couple of days, because they were not disciplined. Discipline was their weakest point. So in the regular and -- army and police forces, of course, there are rules, there is discipline, and I don't deny that, but there was discipline in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When you say reservists the Army of Yugoslavia, who are they? You're talking about them, aren't you? Also, what was the fate of this service in the military since you say that Serbs, Montenegrins, Roma, were all there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reservists in the army are those members who have completed military service and whose names was on the lists in the municipalities, and in case of need, they are mobilised and joined certain units in times of war. Another distinction we -- I would like to make: It was said in Belgrade that these people went to rescue Kosova. "Where are you, brothers? Why aren't you doing anything?" So these were members of this party, and they were sent as volunteers, and they were not on these reservist lists. These were other people. And that is the distinction I would like to make. The reservists are people that can be mobilised, while the paramilitaries were impossible to put under control and disciplined, neither by the army nor by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question was very clear, and you've moved towards volunteers again and paramilitary and police forces. My question was a specific one. Reservists: You said that among them there were Serbs, and Montenegrins, Albanians, and Roma. What happened with the reservists during the NATO action -- or, rather, in the period between the 24th of March up until June 1999? Did the reservists function or not? Were there Albanians and Roma from Kosovo among them, Serbs, et cetera? What happened to that particular branch of the military, that part of the military, that organisational structure of the army?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: 24th of March, 1999; the 12th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large majority of these reservists were deployed and became part of these paramilitary units, the Seselj, the Frenki's. They were not happy with the discipline and the rules in the army, so they had free hand to loot and kill. They were outside the control there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about the reservists who were ethnic Albanians? I mean those joined the paramilitaries because they looked the looting. What about the reservists of Albanian ethnicity? I don't believe you meant them, as well, when you said what you said, that they joined Arkan and whatever.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were very few Albanians. You could count them by the fingers on one hand because they did not report to the units they served before. They refused to join. I mean the Albanians. There were some Roma, and that would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that the Albanian population in Djakovica in that area was a majority as for that military department, an absolute majority?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering the number of people living there, yes, it is true that most of the population was of Albanian ethnicity. However, I would like to reiterate here. They did not respond to the call for mobilisation because the situation was very exacerbated, and it was impossible for Albanians and Serbs and Montenegrins to be in the same unit. It was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I shall thank you for your answer, and I'm not going to ask you anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since the next set of my questions has to do with the organisation and chain of command and will take up quite a bit of time, I believe that this would be a most appropriate moment for the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will have the first break now, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness, Mr. Djordjevic, we're looking ahead to the next witness. Do you think there will be much time to spare for the next witness today? We may simply finish this witness and not move to another one, is the possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that till the end of our working day, we will cross this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll finish this witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we could look to the idea that we won't start another witness. Very well. That's helpful, Mr. Djordjevic, and I'm sure Mr. Stamp will take notice of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I'm grateful. That helps to organise and save the witness having to wait around all day. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As I've already indicated, we will now continue with the chain of command, rules of procedure in the army, military rules since you come from that organisational structure, and I think it would be useful for us in terms of clarifying the case at this trial. Mr. Peraj, in paragraph 6 of your statement you say that the staff of the corps of the Army of Yugoslavia received orders from the ministry of defence in Belgrade. Are you familiar with the chain of command? First of all, let me ask you this: Do you understand the term "chain of command"?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you then tell us, the corps staff or headquarters, who are they responsible to? Who do they report to? They are located in Kosovo. Who do they report to in organisational terms?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the Brigade that I was part of reported to the command of the corps; then the command of the corps reports to the army in Nish; and the army in Nish reports to the Supreme Staff in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You're referring to the 3rd Army in Nis. We will agree about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As regards the chain of command the way that you've explained it to us briefly, could you please tell us, how were reports sent from the field, so from the very scene where something happened? Can you explain to us the reporting procedure about the events in the field? Do you know that, beginning, for instance, with the brigade level.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lowest level in the specific case, the second level, the command of the brigade where I worked, commanded by Djosan, the corps command, part of it was stationed in Gjakove. The reporting can be done in writing because the two commands were close to each other, but also they can report using telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you. In paragraph 28 of your statement -- when I'm referring to the statement, I always refer to the statement of the 8th and 9th of August. It's been admitted into evidence in this case. So if I'm referring to any other statement, I will specify that, but when I say just "statement," I'm talking about the statement that you have in front of you in hard copy. Let me remind you. In paragraph 28 you say: "Colonel Branko Kotur would forward the information to the commander of the 3rd Army in Nis." Who is Colonel Kotur then?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Kotur was in the corps command, in the corps staff, and received orders from the corps commander. He represented the corps in the absence of the commander or his deputy. He had the post of the chief of the operations staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you go on to say that he forwarded the information to the commander of the VJ headquarters or staff in Nis, to General Colonel Dusan Samardzic. How do you know that, and who is Dusan Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Milan Kotur exercised the post, he had --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Milan Kotur or Branko Kotur?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. It's Milan Kotur.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. That means that in paragraph 28 --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Branko Kotur.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Then it's okay. Please do continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers are kindly asked not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His duty was to inform the corps commander either directly or indirectly of what was happening. As for Dusan Samardzic, he was the commander of the 3rd Army in Nish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The information that Colonel Kotur forwarded to Samardzic, was it then forwarded to the ministry of defence in Belgrade? Do you know that, or do you not know that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the task of the army command to forward the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question for you, Mr. Peraj, is this: What kind of training did you do when you were transferred to Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, initially I was the second reporting officer for training and exercise issues. My specific duty was to prepare the soldiers for providing physical guard duty of the barracks and of other features or places where the command of the brigade and its representatives were stationed. I exercised this duty until the very end. I had an assistant who was responsible for the guards in my absence, for example, when I was tasked with other duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next -- my next question for you, Mr. Peraj: The volunteers from Serbia, or paramilitaries, whatever you call them, could they just come from Serbia in a completely unorganised way; in other words, they didn't have to report to anyone in their field upon their arrival, or did they report to somebody and place themselves under somebody's command? How did the chain of command function there when it came to the volunteers coming in from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, and I do not rule out this possibility, they could come in unorganised manner but also in an organised manner. Buses from Nish Expres came; busloads of volunteers came to the cultural centre in Gjakove. Those who came in an organised manner, they had a representative and the necessary documentation proving that they were handed over to the command of the garrison in Gjakove. However, some from the bus would just get off, pick up their suitcases, and walk in the town on their own. Those who came in an organised manner, their personal details were taken down, and they were dislocated to the different units, subordinated to different units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to what you said about the presence of the paramilitaries from various political parties, and I would like to spend some time with them now. I would like you to explain to us how is it that you know that, when and where you saw them, those people who belong to Arkan's Tigers, as you say. If you saw them, when did you see them; where were they billeted; who did they report to; who was in charge of them when they reported or when they arrived in Kosovo; and what is the name of the person in charge who received them in the Army of Yugoslavia once they arrived in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These units, especially the Arkan's unit, were mixed up and fully cooperated with each other, to my knowledge. They were mainly based in the Pashtrik hotel, and I've seen them there with my own eyes. I was even present there for an intervention. The other units, the Seselj units and Frenki units were stationed in some buildings near the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I want to continue asking questions about Arkan's Tigers, so we will then move on to Seselj's men, if we can agree on that. You say that they were billeted in the Pastrik hotel. You're talking about Arkan's Tigers, but my first question was -- I understand what you're saying. They couldn't come to Kosovo without reporting to a certain military staff or organisational unit in order to let them know that they were there. Is this what they did? Did they have to report to the army when they arrived so that everybody knew who they were and that they were there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree to some extent with what you're saying, that they had to report to someone, and probably they did, but I have my doubts in terms of a previous agreement. There must have been a previous agreement for their arrival there. These units did not live well together with the army. They were not cooperative at all with the army. To what I've seen, and I have a lot of information about this, they were always seen in the company of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I think they had an agreement with someone. As I mentioned earlier, if they didn't have such an agreement with someone, these forces would have been fought by both the army and the police. Both the army and the police would have tried to stop them. It was a total anarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you in this regard. Members of Arkan's paramilitary formation, the Tigers, you say that they were there. How did they get supplies with -- of materiel and equipment in the field? How were they supplied with food?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To what I know, they were not supplied with these items directly from the army. They had their own weaponry and equipment. They had different kinds of light weapons. I am sure that they were not provided with foodstuffs by the army. I myself have distributed food to some units. These units were self-organised. The kitchen was there, and they would get themselves food. Even the hotel worked under their orders, served them. They were the ones who were in charge, who issued the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you intervened on one occasion in the Pastrik hotel. What was the name of their commander? If you intervened there, you had to have remembered that because you probably had to talk to him if it was an intervention. And could you please explain to us, what kind of an intervention are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went for an intervention following an order from Colonel Djosan because some soldiers had used alcohol. Alcohol was greatly used in Pashtrik hotel. It's only a street that separates the Pashtrik hotel and the cultural centre. There were gun-shots fired because they were drunk, so my commander said to me, Go and check what's going on, since it was confirmed that there was no attack in question. He said to me, Go and fetch these soldiers, and you can tell them on my behalf that the hotel will no longer serve alcohol drinks. And he advised me not to try and enter into an argument with them. All of them were members of the Arkan army. They were drunk. They knew me by face because I moved around there almost on a daily basis. They offered me a beer. I told them that I could not have a beer because I was on duty, but then one of them said to me, Well, I will throw the beer away then. So in B/C/S I said, I'll just take a sip, then. So I asked them who their boss was, and their reply was, We are all bosses here. You are a good man, so it would be better for you to leave; otherwise, something might happen to you. So I went back. I reported to the commander, and after ten minutes or so Novica Stankovic with six or seven soldiers went there, and his presence was followed by gun-shots fired in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that those were Arkan's Tigers? How can you be certain of that when you say that they did not report to you, that they ignored you?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, they told me in person on several occasions that -- to whom they belonged. That was no secret. They were proud of being Arkan's Tigers. They did not hide this fact from anyone. You may believe me or not, but this was the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Finally, could you just tell me very briefly what kind of light weapons, small arms they had, what kind of uniforms they had, and could you explain to me what you said in your statement when you're talking about Arkan's Tigers; you say that there was a rumour that they were extremely disciplined, but then you mentioned case involving the son of a friend of yours who killed himself because he was a drug addict. But did you have any knowledge then that it was an extremely disciplined military organisation - I'm talking about the Arkan's Tigers - and could you please tell us what kind of clothes they wore and what kind of weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. Could you please again instruct the counsel to ask short and clearly defined questions. Again, these are two, three, four questions in one. I will answer his questions one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How -- or, rather, what kind of small arms did they have?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had automatic rifles, 7.62 millimetres, 9 millimetres; revolvers; and I don't know of anyone not carrying knives, but not knives that are included in the military equipment. Those were knives that were called daggers, the kind that hunters used . They were wearing chains, 60, 70 centimetres long. I didn't see any rocket-launchers or heavy machine-guns. They had light weapons. They also had hand-grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was there some other noticeable detail on all of this in addition to what you've said?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them had the emblem of Arkan's party, the one they used to carry in the war in Bosnia as well. They had their uniforms, which were mainly camouflage. However, some of them would wear mixed civilian and military clothing, civilian trousers and military jackets. They also wore handkerchiefs on their heads. Yes, them, too, the Tigers, black scarves on their heads. I will tell you something else, that they coordinated their actions between each other, and they would stay together because the only place where alcohol was served was Hotel Pashtrik. There were other coffee-shops, as well, but you said never mind them. So that's who they were, people from Frenki's unit and Seselj's unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: From Frenki's and Seselj's unit. What are we discussing now, the Tigers or Frenki's men and Seselj's men? Now I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke about Arkan's Tigers in Pashtrik, but these two also went there, and they stayed together there, and that's why I mentioned it, not for any other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who was this that was engaged in this mutual coordination, Arkan's Tigers or someone beyond that? What are you exactly referring to?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan's Tigers, Seselj's White Eagles, Frenki's units. All of them coordinated amongst themselves. They never argued with each other. They were very well coordinated. I never heard of any problem in their midst. However, who did the coordination, I don't know. It must have been somebody high up. I don't want to give you my ideas here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know. But of course. My question at the outset had to do with alcohol and discipline. You mentioned that you had heard that this was the case among Arkan's Tigers, rather, that they did not drink alcohol at all and that they had maximum discipline among their army ranks. Was that your impression?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. In terms of discipline, they were a little more disciplined. Arkan's people were more disciplined. However, they would drink until they were totally drunk, and I know this for a fact, and I saw them with my own eyes together in Pashtrik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Finally, look at paragraph 42 of your statement. Of course, it is P313 for the umpteenth time today. Paragraph 42. How do you explain the beginning of this sentence? You say that: "I had no contact with the White Eagles or Tigers other than bumping into the Tigers once at the Pashtrik Hotel in Djakovica." So you did not see them. You had no contact with them. You bumped into one of the Tigers. Now, I really wonder how the interpreters are going to interpret that. Quite an expression, isn't it? Bumping, yes, bumping into the Tigers. Right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I did not have direct contact with them. I just saw them in the street, but I did not speak to them. I mentioned what happened in Pashtrik. Apart from that, there's nothing else. I saw them in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's a good answer. Fine. Tell me, camouflage uniforms, what colour were they? I mean the Tigers' uniforms.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very similar to the army uniform with very slight differences. The colours were a little lighter. It was a camouflage uniform but lighter colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did they wear any kind of caps or helmets or anything of the kind or nothing whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them were not wearing anything on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did they have any radio equipment? Every member of the Tigers, was that on their chests?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones I ran into, I did not see them having any radio equipment. I did see some in Prishtina, but they were commanders in 1997, 1998, and I remember seeing them with such equipment, very sophisticated ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was the name of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan's, party?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall it now. I used to know the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the emblem of the Tigers looked like? They wore it, and I'm not going to say how and where they wore it, but what did this emblem look like, the one that the Tigers wore?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember for the moment. It's been a long time. Some of them I know, but I'm not sure, so I don't want to assume here, make assumptions. However, the most important thing is that they admitted themselves to be part of that force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, do you know in what actions they took part, and if so, where? The specific area, please. I'm referring to Arkan's Tigers.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took part in Meje, in Meje, together with other forces as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Within your brigade, did you have an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intelligence officer? No, I don't think so. A security officer, yes, but he could have covered both fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did the security officer know about the presence of Arkan's Tigers out in the field; and if so, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seregj Perovic was the security officer. And to be honest, you didn't ask the question, but I will say this: I think that he knew about everything, and he told me who belonged to which and from whom should I be careful and protect myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We are going to move on to Seselj's White Eagles. When did they arrive?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they arrived by the end of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Gjakove. Maybe they arrived earlier in another part of the country, but in Gjakove they arrived in 1998. It was before New Year's Eve.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how did they get there? What did they use for transportation?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how they got there and what means of transportation they used. I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know, then? How do you know that they arrived?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they could be seen in Gjakove, in the streets, that they had arrived. They did not just drop from the sky. Of course, they came from somewhere. Whether it was an organised way of arriving or not, I don't know. I know what vehicles they used when they moved around in Gjakove, yes, but how they arrived, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Tell me, did they report to your army, to your command, that they had arrived? Did they place themselves under your command or someone else's command, if you know, and you were in Djakovica at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, because if they had reported to the command, we would have a list, a register of some sort, and we would have to support them with food supplies, weapons, vehicles. Please believe me that they had better vehicles. The members of these units, they had better vehicles than the commander of the brigade, much more sophisticated vehicles that they had looted from people, they had taken away from people. I don't know where from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So you did work on establishing the provenance of these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These vehicles were not army or police vehicles. They were vehicles that had been looted from the people, very good jeeps and Mercedes cars, and they didn't care what they did to those people. If those people so much as tried to resist, they would be killed on the spot. Of course, the army and the police did mobilise some vehicles, civilian vehicles, but, however, they would give a certificate that this was taken for a temporary period for the needs of the army or the police. However, unfortunately, they were never returned, but we won't enter into this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Actually, we've moved in the completely wrong direction. This question is of really no relevance to this case. I do apologise to the Honourable Trial Chamber and to my colleague Mr. Stamp. However, I got carried away by what you were saying, although that is impermissible, so I do apologise to all concerned. We will agree that the Serbs organise themselves in different parties, and they arrived in Kosovo without the knowledge of the military and without any kind of organisation. Everybody was waging his own little war in Kosovo and perhaps elsewhere too. No one reported to anyone. No one didn't -- know officially that they were there. No one provided them with food, materiel, technical resources. Every army brought in their own resources, their own vehicles, their own food and so on and so forth. Will you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I'm afraid this is another speech. I think I'll just have to interrupt you each time you launch into one from now on, or we'll find we can't finish. You had the evidence from the witness, so I don't think you need to try to summarise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the witness agree with me that political parties in Serbia had their own armies, and they went into Kosovo and they acted independently without any kind of liaison with others? At least that is what I infer on the basis of what the witness has been telling us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to assist with that, Mr. Peraj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Honourable gentlemen, I -- I'm not saying that they were armies. They were mobilised forces by political parties, and my personal opinion is that the chairmen of these parties coordinated with somebody high up on these issues because otherwise -- because had it been otherwise, the army would have acted against these forces and would not have allowed these forces to arrive there. On the basis of these facts, I think that there was a preliminary agreement between them to send forces. They called them voluntary forces, volunteers. However, the situation on the ground was completely different. Even if they had previous understanding between each other, they did not act upon such understanding or agreement. This would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question is: As for the volunteers -- I mean, I'm not going to call them Arkan's men or Seselj's men or Russians or whatever. I'm just going to call them volunteers. Did you, as the army, receive them in Djakovica? You explained something to us, that you were writing down the names and surnames of these people, et cetera. Did they go through any kind of training? Could you please respond to that? That has to do with what you stated today, namely, that you kept some kind of records of volunteers who were coming in, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a situation of war, there is no training because there is no time for training. These volunteers had been previously trained in Bosnia, Croatia, and wherever they came from, most of them. There were cases when they came and they registered, and the next day they were sent to the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is why they came; right? But did you register all of them? Was it possible for anyone to enter the area of responsibility of your brigade without you knowing about that? Was that feasible at all?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Illegally, yes, not legally. However, you reminded me of something here. The same unit that came as volunteers, they said, and I heard them myself and I quote: We have been told to stay in town, and if there is need, we will stay in town and we won't go to Koshare. Djosan told them, Thank you for coming, but this is where we need you now. And everybody left and went to town. The military police was engaged then to go and catch them wherever they were. They didn't want to come for the proper patriotic reasons. They had come for other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a matter that I don't wish to discuss. Quite simply, I got the answer that I was interested in, so tell me: How did you make a distinction between the members of Seselj's party, the volunteers of Seselj's party and others? What kind of weapons did they have? What kind of side-arms?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of Seselj's people, almost none of them carried automatic rifles. Knives dominated, and pistols. They changed their uniforms almost daily. Where they got them, I don't know. Military uniforms, police uniforms, combined uniforms, headscarves, different kinds of emblems. They were tattooed on their bodies everywhere, and they showed everything very openly, and they were singing songs. And I apologise again to the interpreters because I will confuse them. [Witness sings]. It's a song about Seselj, and I suspect that they were drug users, heavy drug users. I heard from my colleagues that they used a lot of drugs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So your colleagues mingled with them. Could you please give us some names of those colleagues of yours who told you that about Seselj's men, first names, last names?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly the security officer. In our everyday conversations, he told me about their behaviour, yes, and he told me to be careful and not to use my jeep because they would cake it away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about Officer Perovic; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My last question about Seselj's guard, the White Eagles, is: Do you know who their commander was, and what actions did they take part in, if any?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the name of the commander of the Seselj's unit. However, I'm 100 percent sure that they took part in the -- in Meje and in Korenice, but also in town, in looting houses and setting them alight.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, who is Franko Simatovic? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never met him. I know that he was the commander of the so-called Frenki's, named after him. I know that he was in charge of this unit when it was formed initially, before it arrived in Kosova. Frenki Sumatovic, Simatovic, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot has been said about him on television, newspapers, media in general, but personally I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of a unit was that, Frenki's men? Who were they? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, he was the commander of this unit, which was a special unit, Special Anti-Terrorist Unit. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you this: Let's say from the 1st of January, 1999, until June, the 12th of June, 1999, was there a Special Anti-Terrorist Unit under the command of Frenki Simatovic, Franko Simatovic, or was there perhaps something else? Had it already been disbanded by that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, but it would take me quite some time to elaborate and explain this. If you give me permission to give an elaborated answer, then I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in existence at that time or not? That's my question. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Gjakove specifically, there were Frenki's forces, and I will explain to you how they were organised in Gjakove. Not all the unit of Frenki was in Gjakove. There were certain persons tasked with mobilising other persons into their own units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, if you say that Frenki's men were in Djakovica, and that's what you're saying, who was their commander? Who was his name?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know their commander. I was told by my colleagues, and they mentioned this very often, a certain colonel by the name of Kovacevic who was assigned with the task of coordinating these forces. This is what I heard. Personally, I cannot ascertain or deny this information. However, their presence in Gjakove was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question: Where were Frenki's forces, members of that special unit, billeted?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
