utterances.text: Behind the Vllaznimi stadium in a building. They removed the civilian population from that building and moved themselves in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, where were Seselj's White Eagles billeted?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a building which is opposite to the Hajdar Dushi gymnasium. There were several military apartments in these buildings in the past. That's where they were mostly seen, but they did change their location often. That was like a point of a -- a meeting point for them, close the to the army centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, do you have any knowledge of Frenki's men participating in any actions?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear of an operation that -- in which they participated on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to look at D001-5784, it's the English version; and D001-5782, that's in Albanian. This is the statement of the 17th of June, 1999, that the witness gave, signed, and wrote in his own hand. And in the English version, we in fact have a translation of that handwritten statement. Could you please look at this statement in English, Mr. Peraj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to look at the signature in the Albanian version. I want to ask Mr. Peraj if it is indeed his signature, so could that part of the statement please be shown on the screen. It's at the end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement in handwriting, first of all, that is not my handwriting. I think that the signature has been falsified, forged perfectly, perfidiously. I do have notes, not here with me here today, and you can see from my notes that this is not my handwriting. Just a small detail as proof. It says here, "Deklaroi." I would never write it like that. I would write it with a J in the end. So that's why I'm saying that my signature has been forged perfidiously. It's not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who handed this document over to the OTP of the Tribunal, this forgery? So you're claiming this is a forgery?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely. That's not my handwriting. We should be clear on this, and the person who sent this must know who did the forging. It's a complete forgery. I have my suspicions about who could have done this, but I'm not going to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is not of interest to us, perhaps some other proceedings, but let me ask you this: Mr. Peraj, you testified in the Milutinovic et al case. You gave a number of statements. Were you ever shown this statement by the Prosecution since my learned friend Mr. Stamp referred to all the statements, to the sublimation of all the statements, and the sublimation is contained in P313, so did you ever state that this statement of the 17th of June, 1999, apparently written in some kind of block capitals, is a total forgery as you stated here today?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just state -- may I just intervene --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will let the witness answer first, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the statement on the right-hand side, I'm telling you that this is not my handwriting, and it is a forgery, pure forgery. And my signature, too, has been forged perfidiously, copied. The statements that I gave to the investigators --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever, ever signed a handwritten statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness -- or, rather, Your Honour, I insist on getting an answer to that. Before giving the floor to the Prosecution, could I please have the answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Answer to what, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, have you ever before today say anywhere that this statement -- or, rather, that this signature is not yours and that this is all a total forgery? So did you ever say that ever before today?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see a statement in handwriting. I don't know where you got it from. Maybe you should tell us who provided you with this forgery. This is not my statement, and you can prove this. I can bring you notebooks with my handwriting, and you can have an expert in handwriting do the analysis, and you will see that this is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Stamp, you've been waiting a moment to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the witness was about to say what I wanted to say at line 47 -- at page 47, line 15, when he said, "The statements I gave to the investigators ..." I think he was about to say what I will say now. Counsel for the Defence has said that I represented at some point in time that in the statement we have in evidence as the witness's statement is a sublimation of all witness's statements. That is not correct, and I wish to just correct that for the record, and that is at yesterday at page 1182, lines 18 to 23. The statements which we referred to, which the Prosecution refers to and has used and tendered in this case are statements which were taken by officers of the OTP of this Tribunal and not all possible statements which the witness might have made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you for correcting that. I must say I didn't understand that from what you said yesterday, and I'm sure that will help Mr. Djordjevic. The statement Exhibit P313, Mr. Stamp says is, as it were, a putting together of statements made by the witness to the Office of the Prosecutor, not of other statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is also a document that we received practically from our colleagues from the Prosecution, and I am really happy I hear the witness say this, and this is why I'm going ask for this document to be admitted into evidence in its entirety, the document that the witness claims is a complete forgery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment, he says it isn't his statement. We can mark it for identification and keep it in the court record, but it won't be an exhibit until somebody can identify what it is. It will be marked for identification, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00031 MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Peraj, you've been patiently waiting to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just shortly, Your Honour, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see anything which is in conflict with what I've said in my previous statements. However, this is not my handwriting. I just wanted to tell you that I didn't see any threat from this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I don't think we need to bother further with that, Mr. Peraj. Thank you for that. Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As regards the Territorial Defence, just one short question. You said in the statement of yours, that's paragraph 36, that the Territorial Defence involved people from the ages of 15 to 65. Did you really mean that, from 15 to 65 for the Territorial Defence? Is it true that you said that simply --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eighteen to 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's more sensible. So we have that corrected now. Could you explain to us the difference between the Territorial Defence and the civilian protection? That's paragraph 37. You are talking about both.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civil protection is under the umbrella of Territorial Defence, and they have their own specific tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the operational commander of the Territorial Defence for the Gjakove municipality was in fact Nikola Micunovic, aka -- well, the nickname has nothing to do with his real name, but could you please tell us, what does it mean, "operational commander"? How are we to understand that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you give me the number of the paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thirty-seven, Mr. Peraj, line 3. We can see that he was in fact in peacetime just -- he played just an administrative role, but what was he doing during the war? What is it, the operational commander of Territorial Defence, and who did he report to? You say that here. You say that he reported to Mayor Stanojevic. So who is Micunovic, and who is Stanojevic? But first of all, my first question to you is: "Operational commander of the Territorial Defence," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander of the Territorial Defence in Gjakove, for Gjakove municipality, that is, was Momcilo Stanojevic, while Nikola Micunovic was the commander of the mobilised forces of the Territorial Defence, which was under the command of the mayor of the municipality, which in war-time assumes the role of the commander of these Territorial Defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So let's clear this up. Stanojevic or Micunovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Micunovic was the person who reported to Stanojevic. However, the operational part of the work, of the job, he was responsible for the operational part of the work. This is the meaning of the operational commander that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that they reported -- that Micunovic reported to Djosan, does that mean that the Territorial Defence had placed itself under the command of the Yugoslav Army? Is that how I should understand it?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, in a municipality where there is a military district or military formation, rather, like a brigade, which is not a small formation, the other forces that are involved in military activities fall under the command of the garrison commander, with the exception of cases when it is has been ordered previously to do otherwise, because it is possible for an officer or a higher-ranking officer to come and be assigned there in that district and take over the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And please tell me, the reservists and the Territorial Defence, during the war did they operate together, or were they also operating separately without any particular coordination?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We should understand each other here. Reservists were mobilised by both Territorial Defence and the army. Therefore, the Territorial Defence, the army, and the police had to have full coordination between themselves. However, the army is more responsible vis-a-vis the Territorial Defence units. Whatever the case, they have to closely cooperate in the territory, that is in municipality, in the municipality in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the essence of my question. In practice, did they operate like a single organisation, the territorials, the Territorial Defense, the reservists of the army? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It resembled a single organisation, but in reality it was different. Nikola Micunovic was involved in a verbal argument with Djosan about this issue. So I cannot speak of good relations here because something was not functioning in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's wrap up because I can see that we have to have our break. Could you please tell us: Mr. Micunovic, he was a retired military man or something else, and then he was reactivated? What was it?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that he had been retired. Well, even if that was the case, quite normally he would have been mobilised. He worked in the sector which, in B/C/S, is Vojni Odsek, a military district in Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did he have any rank?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What rank?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was a first class captain at least, but I think he was promoted to major at the time. I don't remember, as I said, what was his initial rank before he was promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I suggest that we take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. And we resume at 1.00, and you will bear in mind the need to leave some time to Mr. Stamp for re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I please address you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to the best of my ability to cut my cross-examination short in order to allow this witness to complete his testimony before this court today, but in light of the importance of the circumstances that I wanted to ask him about, I would like to ask you - and this concerns, also, the interpreters who are present here - I have learnt that there is no trial scheduled for this afternoon, and I realise that we will need more time because Mr. Stamp has to have the right to re-examine the witness, but could release extend, perhaps, our sitting time today so that the witness's testimony could be completed today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we're not in a position that we can simply adjust to take this afternoon's sitting because different interpreters are arranged for this afternoon's sitting and because commitments have been made by Judges in other matters. What we can do to try and help is to extend to the maximum edge of the present tapes, which will give us perhaps another ten minutes, and that is all we can do. So you'll just have to move as quickly and as to the point as you can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will then continue with my cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, could you please tell me, what do you know about the relationship between the last name that you mentioned in your statement, Adamovic, and the last name of Kovacevic? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Adamovic was a MUP commander. I wanted to have an appointment with him once for personal reasons, and I was told that he was ill and was in Belgrade at the time. He was replaced by Colonel Kovacevic. And I will say this again - this is what I heard - Kovacevic was acting as -- in his place for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: For a time, or did Kovacevic remain there until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He stayed there for quite some time, as far as I know, but I'm not sure about later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, according to the information that the Defence has, Mr. Kovacevic was appointed after Adamovic, the chief of the Djakovica SUP. Can you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't know, but it could be as you say. I don't deny -- I can't deny that he was. Maybe he was given that post, but I don't know. However, I know that the colonel's name was mentioned several times in our conversations and in our briefing sessions in the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's strange that you don't know that since you spoke about your briefings, the briefings between the army and the police in great detail, so it's strange that you don't know that since you were in Djakovica at the time. My next question has to do with paragraph 22 of your statement. I would like you to give you this reference so that we can cut this short. You say that in the area of Djakovica there were over 170 tanks, and then in the same paragraph you say that you know that the man who worked at the gas station said that in late April he fuelled 60 tanks that day. Is it possible that there were so many tanks at the time when the NATO air-strikes were going on, and how do you know that there were so many tanks there at that time? And nothing else, just that.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to fueling, which is Serb is Tankiranje, there was a non-commissioned officer who told me about that. I can't remember his name now. It was his duty to supply petrol. And he told me that there would be a lot to do in the future days, as well, to supply petrol to other tanks. I'm very sure about that because when the convoy formed to withdraw, I can tell you that there could have been even more than I already said now. These tanks did not move from the places they were deployed, especially after the NATO bombing started. They did not move from their positions for security reasons and also because they did not need to use them. The Prizren-Gjakove-Decane-Peje axis was the most important one because of an eventual attack from the Republic of Albania. So from earlier on, tanks were positioned along this line that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clear this up. This number of tanks, we're talking about Djakovica or the whole of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the whole of Kosova, just Gjakove, Decane, and the other part towards Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Based on what information did the Yugoslav Army expect attacks from the Republic of Albania, and who was supposed to attack?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was being said that if the bombing would not be successful, then ground forces, NATO ground forces, would come and would enter through that territory. That was what was said, but it never came true. That's why the preparations were made before such a thing could happen. There were many things said about these things on television, in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: A brief question for you, Mr. Peraj. Were there any incursions from the Republic of Albania by various armed groups? Who did those groups belong to, if you know, and when did this happen, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, there were groups that crossed the border, various groups of civilians but also members of the KLA. They crossed from Albania into the territory of Kosova. As regards regular forces of the Albanian army, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question, Mr. Peraj, is this: After the Army of Yugoslavia left, did you give any statements to the KLA police? And when I'm asking you this, before you give me your answer, could you please look at paragraph 108 of your statement. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please look at D001-5900, that's the Albanian version; and D001-5907, that's the English version. And before we get this on the screen, could we please ask the witness to look very carefully at this statement in the Albanian language and to tell us this: After the usher has presented the statement to him in full, the first page, second page, third page and so on, to say whether this is a statement that he gave or not. It's in B/C/S. Fine. The witness under understands the language. Could he just tell me whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether this is indeed the statement. Let me just check once again. No, that's not the statement. Just a moment, please. D001-5900. Yes, that's the Albanian version. And in the English version -- in the English language, 5907, D001-5907. Yes, that's correct. That's it. Could the witness please be shown this statement, all the pages in the Albanian language from page 1 to the last page. If he could tell us whether this is indeed his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to say that you can see that this handwriting is different from the previous one. Secondly, yes, I wrote this myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Could we then have on our screens D001-5925.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm in a rush and I forgot it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00032, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have D001-5925 in the English language; and in the Albanian language, it's D001-5929. It is the transcript of a purported audio and video recording of a conversation with Nike Peraj, who is present here. So I would like to ask him if he is aware of this transcript, if he knows anything about it. [In English] In English, as far as I can see, it is only summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please look at this transcript in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not in Albanian. However, it's not a problem. I would like to have it zoomed in, please. Your Honours, may I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave a statement in the premises of this Tribunal to two prosecutors. I can't remember the name -- their names. There was a lady with them, and I also gave a statement to -- Paolo Stocchi I think was his name. So I gave a statement, and it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't receive translation. Now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Okay. The witness said he gave two statements in this Tribunal, the first two prosecutors, there was a lady with him, and he also gave a statement to a Paolo Stocchi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. This was in the presence of Paolo Stocchi. I gave statement to the Belgrade prosecutors here in the Tribunal, in the presence of Paolo Stocchi. I gave them a statement about the things that I had also said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the time when you gave this statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember the date. About two years ago. I think that Milosevic died, or maybe Babic died in that period. It was at that time, but I can't give you the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: March 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. [Interpretation] Your Honour, now I would like to tender this statement into evidence. Now I don't want to be asking any more questions about it because we don't have enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Djordjevic. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we get to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This document, there's no translation of it in the language of the Tribunal -- in the language of the Tribunal. I understand that what we're seeing here is not a translation of the document but someone's summary. So it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document will be marked for identification together with the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But then in that case, Your Honour, since we have a summary here, can we then submit a request for a full translation of this document into English and then to have it admitted into evidence in this case once the translation has been received?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. You've anticipated very well. That's what can occur, but you will need to ask the Translation Unit to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00033 MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm grateful to you, Mr. President, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you this. This is the first time, Mr. Peraj, that you mentioned the forward command post of the police. If I'm not mistaken, it was a prayer house, and it is in Lokaci Dusna [phoen], the village of Lokaci Dusna. Now, I would like you to tell us this: You told us that you didn't speak to anyone but that you saw a police general there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell me -- can you describe what this man looked like?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope you won't get offended by this. He was about as heavily built as you, a little bit taller. He had grey hair, almost white, white facial features, red blotches on his face. This is how he looked. He was wearing a camouflage uniform with the brown colour dominating, the same as the army, but it was very good design, and he kept his rank markings. Generally -- on the shoulders. Generally, in times of war they don't keep their ranks, they don't show them, but they felt safe there, it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, apart from concluding that the gentleman was well-built and looked good, I would like to ask you this: Did you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never mentioned his name because the person I was with addressed him as chief or boss, and they never used names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, can you tell me why this is the first time you've said this? Until now, you've never mentioned the forward command post of Dusna, of the police. This is the first time you're doing this. Why? What is the reason you're doing this for the very first time now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours. Your Honours, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In his evidence before and in his statements, he has mentioned the forward command post. As a matter of fact, in one of the maps that we tendered, which was a map that he said is based on a map that he has drawn and is a map from, I think, the year 2004, the forward command post of the police is marked on it. I can't remember the exhibit number, but that is one of the maps that was tendered on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Does that help your recollection, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is Friday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] No, I wouldn't have done that if I remembered. I know it's Friday afternoon, Your Honour. I would like to say that the witness never did mention, first of all, this kind of agreement or discussion in the staff, and that is the main reason why I'm asking him that and saying that it's the first time. Secondly, does the witness know that it was only the army that had the so-called forward command post, whereas the police does not really do that kind of thing in its activities and its operations. Perhaps the witness called it that, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we can see if the witness can comment on that, Mr. Djordjevic. It's suggested, Mr. Peraj, that the -- only the army has forward command posts, not the police. Is that something that affects your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the question. It is possible that -- it is possible because that brigade is not a small brigade. It had the task of cleaning or mopping up the terrain because there were allegedly terrorists there. This was a brigade that was engaged in specific conditions or circumstances, and it plays the same role automatically, and they have their own command staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying this is an army brigade or a police brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A police brigade for special warfare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you think it may be because of its special function that it used a forward command post. That's the point of your answer, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because someone has to command with this brigade. Someone has to follow the operations closely of this brigade, and this was an elite brigade, a strong brigade in terms of men, and it is completely understanding that a higher-ranking officer shall command with such a brigade. This was a very important area for the Yugoslav State because it was very close to the border with Albania. Before the war and during the war, the tasks were such and the subordination was such so that everybody should know who commands with which unit, who belongs to which unit. So this was a special brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why is this the first time that he mentions attendance at such a meeting with such high-ranking commanders? The witness never stated this before. Even what my colleague Mr. Stamp said, that he marked forward command post of the police on the map, I could agree with that, but never before have I come across this kind of a statement of his where he speaks of this police command post where he sees the general and all these other people who are discussing matters there, including other people who have very high rank and so on and so forth. Why is this the first time that he's saying this? Why has he never said so before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't asked specifically about this brigade in the past, just like you're asking me now. That's the reason. There's no other reason. I wasn't asked in details before, Who did you see there, how did they look, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No one's asking you now in any kind of detail either. This is your statement. How is it that --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question led me to this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No. That's what you claim in your testimony in direct examination. It's not that I provoked you to say this. You had already said it. But my next question - our time is limited - the first time you say that this was a meeting that you attended when the massacre in Meje was planned. Tell me, were you personally in attendance there at that meeting, and in what capacity did you attend that meeting? I never saw this before. I never saw you claiming anywhere that you attended a meeting where the massacre in Meje was being planned literally. You are saying now for the first time that you attended a meeting where the massacre in Meje was being planned.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not convened there to have a meeting. It was a meeting for other things. Persons mentioned in the statement were supposed to take part in the funeral of an officer -- of an officer who had been killed in Meje, and I was living there at the time. I had my guards. I had people from the military police with me there. These people came. I knew Momir Stojanovic very well. Perovic was with me there. I was there in the corridor of the building when they entered. He stopped for a chat with me, so at this meeting this thing was mentioned. It was said at the meeting that at least 100 people should be killed and the whole territory burnt down. I've mentioned this in my previous statement as well. At the time, I understood this to be a reaction of the anger. The first cousin of Prascevic is Momir's wife. They were somehow in-laws. This is how I understood it at the time, as a reaction to an anger, but unfortunately what was said there came true. I'm not saying that he planned it, but I heard this being said, and unfortunately, it really happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about all of this because I did not see that that was your testimony earlier on, Mr. Peraj. Now my next question: The first time you say that at 2200 hours on the 27th of April - I'm going to slow down because this is way too fast for the interpreters - at the cultural centre, across -- over the shoulder of Zdravko Vinter, you said that you read a report on an operation carried out, and it is mentioned that 74 terrorists were killed in -- and 68 in Korenica. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement of 2000, in paragraph 31, your statement of the 18th of April, 2000, you say that four days after the Meje incident, you saw on this computer this information that I put to you a few moments ago concerning the terrorists who were killed in Meje and Korenica, but you do not refer to Zdravko Vinter in your statement of the 18th of April, 2000. Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this paragraph, I've made a correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, if he is going to direct the witness to some previous statement he's made in a statement, I think counsel should show the witness the statement and quote precisely what the witness is purported to be saying in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would not disagree with you, Mr. Stamp, but as a matter of practical convenience, we have often been able to proceed successfully in a less formal way, but -- The witness points out he's corrected the paragraph, Mr. Djordjevic. It's paragraph 31, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the number of this statement is D001-5788, and D001-5797. [Interpretation] So before we actually see it, I'm just going to try to get an answer from Mr. Peraj as to why that was not stated then. I know what the witness did, correct, but I'm asking him why did he state what he stated then? Why was it not handled this way, as he ultimately corrected it? What's the reason?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you remember what was in that statement, Mr. Peraj, or do you need to look at it first?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is on the screen, Your Honours. [In English] In B/C/S, not in Albanian, as far as I can see, but I think that there is not any problem about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it paragraph 31 that we should turn to?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we will get paragraph 31 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yep. No, it is not 31. It's at paragraph 50 and 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you saying it's no longer 31 but 5-0?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifty, 66, paragraph 41, and my colleague Mr. Stamp mentioned a supplementary statement where the witness changed all the things that he said in those paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Albanian version, I'm told, has some 34 paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And may I just say, Your Honour, may I just say that I said no such thing. I did not mention in a statement where the witness changed all the things that he said in those paragraphs. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In my hand is a statement dated the 18th of April, 2000, Mr. Djordjevic. Is that the one that you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. I want to know why he did not mention Mr. Vinter at the time at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there a particular paragraph that deals with this event?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It's, I think, page 5 of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll see whether page 5 can be brought up onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the B/C/S there is no that. It is about Major Zivkovic and -- but in that statement, for sure -- I have to find a hard copy because I also can't see on the ... Yeah. That's the page 7, in fact. [Interpretation] Second paragraph starts: "[In English] Four days later, the incident in Meje, I saw in the computer we had at a cultural centre that 68 men were killed in Meje and 74 men in Korenica ..." and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In his statement, in his -- [Interpretation] of the 8th and 9th of August admitted into evidence under 92 ter in full, the witness mentions Officer Vinter, and he says that he noted that he saw this report looking over his shoulder. Why did he not say that at the time but only in this statement? So why this discrepancy? It will turn out to be important.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just pause at that question. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at what has been shown to the witness here in the statement of 2000 or what is written: "Four days later, the incident in Meje, I saw in the computer we had at the cultural centre, 68 were killed --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're about to deal with that, Mr. Stamp. We're about to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If my friend is representing to the witness that the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, if you could be seated, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just make the point with respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please be seated, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not very well. If you're asked to be seated, be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now be seated, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djordjevic, you want to put to the witness that in paragraph 31 he has not mentioned the name of a particular person, Vinter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. When we're talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the 18th of April statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Peraj, if you look at paragraph 31 in front of you, you've described seeing a report about these bodies at the cultural centre on a computer. Can you give an explanation why in that paragraph you did not mention the name of the person Vinter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did mention his name both during my testimony in the Milosevic trial and Milutinovic trial in this court. It's not the first time I mention his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When you gave this statement in April 2000, when you were dealing with the subject matter in paragraph 31, is there a reason why you did not mention the name of that particular person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, I'm not clear either. I know that I mentioned his name, and I don't know why it doesn't appear there. I state here with full responsibility that the person behind the computer was Zdravko Vinter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is there anything further, Mr. Djordjevic, you want to ask about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I am satisfied with this answer, and I will move on to my next question. My next question is Seregj Perovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this your last question, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my last topic, Seregj Perovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And how long would you expect to be on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Till 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid that is too long for the tape. We're going to have to conclude the evidence on Monday, and on Monday you may expect to have ten minutes, not five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Stamp, I had to be rather abrupt with you earlier. There are times when if the Chamber asks you to be quiet or be seated in the middle of questioning, you must accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, and I'm prepared to accept it, as I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, even at this moment your mood suggests that you may not be, but we will put that aside, and please understand that if you are asked to sit, you should sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At some other time, you may want to raise the matter again. Now, the point you were going to make, as you've half-indicated it, was very obvious to the Chamber, and there was no need to make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I tried to in this questioning pin down the one question that was being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just apologise to the Court, but I thought at the time, at that time, that I was raising something that it was my duty to raise, to stand on my feet and say it, but I intend to abide by the rulings of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can well understand that was your position, and this is why we are parting in good harmony I trust, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are now, unfortunately, having to continue your evidence on Monday, I'm afraid, Mr. Peraj. We have a time limitation that we can sit, and we've reached just beyond that time. Our tapes will run out at any moment. So I'm afraid we cannot finish your evidence. There will be more questions from Mr. Djordjevic, more from Mr. Stamp. The Chamber may have some. You need to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It is not possible for me to continue my evidence on Monday. If I am forced to, then that's a different story, but unfortunately, it's not possible for me. As of Tuesday, I've made it known to the officers that my wife is ill. She's suffering from high blood pressure. Personally, I don't have anything against coming and testifying on Monday and staying here for the weekend. I'm even available in the evenings. I know that it's not possible in this court, but because of my wife, please believe me that it really isn't possible for me. However, if you obliged me to come and testify, then I will do that. If you issue an order about that, then I will do. Otherwise, I'd rather not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for making your position clearly known. You can see the position we have reached and the difficulty. I am unaware of the flight schedules that would enable you to get home, but I can say that it is anticipated that your evidence on Monday would be finished by 10.30 in the morning, and it may be possible to arrange a flight for you then to be home by Monday evening. We're sorry about that, Mr. Peraj, but that is the way the matter has gone. We now adjourn until Monday morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 23rd day of February, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.59 p.m.,
